name: Oxford University, English Learning Independent of Paris
summary: Oxford University develops from a cluster of schools in the city, growing rapidly after Henry II's 1167 expulsion of English scholars from Paris (during a dispute with France). By the early 13th century it has recognizable institutional structure, master regents, student nations, and academic halls. Roger Bacon's experimental natural philosophy (1250s-1280s) and Wycliffe's theology (1370s) demonstrate Oxford's capacity for intellectual innovation outside Parisian Scholasticism.

_quarry.structural_significance: Oxford's development gives England an indigenous university that trains royal administrators, common lawyers, and eventually reformers independently of continental influence; the common law emphasis (lawyers trained at the Inns of Court adjacent to Oxford) creates a distinctive English legal culture separate from the Roman law tradition dominant on the continent; Oxford's later Lollard connection demonstrates how universities could become centers of theological dissent
